name: THE LITTLE SPROUTS ON THE PRAIRIE BURGER

recipe.history:
Brussels sprouts — Brassica oleracea var. gemmifera — belong to the same species as cabbage, broccoli, kale, and cauliflower, all of which were developed through millennia of selective cultivation from a single wild ancestor native to the Mediterranean coastline. The Brussels sprout as we know it — the small, compact, cabbage-like bud growing along a tall central stalk — was developed in the Low Countries of northern Europe, almost certainly in the region around Brussels, Belgium, from which it takes its name. Written records of Brussels sprout cultivation in Belgium date to at least the 13th century, and by the 16th century the vegetable was well established throughout the region. The cool, damp climate of Belgium and the Netherlands proved ideal for sprout cultivation, and Flemish farmers refined the variety over centuries to produce the tight, leafy buds we recognize today. The sprout spread across northern Europe — to France, Germany, and Britain — largely following trade routes and the movement of gardeners and seeds. In Britain, Brussels sprouts became almost culturally inseparable from the Christmas dinner, boiled to a soft, sulfurous state and endured rather than enjoyed by generations of children. It was only when cooks began roasting them at high heat — caramelizing the outer leaves, crisping the cut faces, and reducing the sulfurous compounds through dry heat rather than concentrating them in boiling water — that Brussels sprouts revealed what they had always been capable of.

Brussels sprouts arrived in North America with European settlers and were grown in kitchen gardens throughout the colonial period, but they did not gain widespread commercial cultivation until the 20th century. California became the center of American Brussels sprout production by the mid-century, with the fog-drenched coast near Santa Cruz proving climatically perfect for the crop. For decades, Brussels sprouts were the punchline of American vegetable humor — the thing children pushed to the edge of the plate, the symbol of dietary suffering. The transformation of Brussels sprouts' reputation is one of the great stories of American food culture in the late 2000s and early 2010s. Restaurants, led by the nose-to-tail and farm-to-table movements, began serving roasted Brussels sprouts as a side dish, and the response was immediate and dramatic. Crispy, caramelized, tossed with bacon, fish sauce, lemon zest, or hot honey, roasted Brussels sprouts became one of the most ordered vegetable dishes in the country. Shaved raw Brussels sprouts appeared in salads. Brussels sprout leaves were fried to chips. The vegetable had been rehabilitated entirely, and its place on a burger — shaved, roasted crispy, piled high — was a natural culmination of that journey.

I was a committed Brussels sprout skeptic for the first twenty or so years of my life. My introduction to them, like most people's of my generation, was boiled, gray-green, smelling faintly of wet wool, placed on a plate with the authority of someone who expected them to be eaten. I ate them. I did not enjoy them. The conversion happened at a dinner party when I was in my late twenties, where the host served roasted Brussels sprouts with crispy prosciutto and a squeeze of lemon as the first thing on the table. I picked one up skeptically, bit through the shatteringly crisp outer leaf into the creamy, nutty interior, and experienced a genuine culinary revelation. This was the same vegetable? The Maillard reaction, working on the cut faces and the outer leaves, had transformed them into something almost meaty — caramelized, rich, with a slight bitterness that was now a feature rather than a flaw. I went home that night and roasted my own, standing at the oven eating them off the baking sheet. They have been my favorite vegetable ever since. They belong on this burger, and nowhere more rightly.

A medium rare patty — 130–135°F — is the ideal canvas for the assertive flavors of roasted Brussels sprouts. The slight bitterness of the caramelized sprout echoes and complements the Maillard browning on the surface of the beef; the nuttiness of the roasted brassica mirrors the nuttiness of rendered beef fat. Cook the patty beyond medium rare and you lose the dialogue — the dried, tight protein of an overcooked patty simply competes with the Brussels sprouts' intensity rather than partnering with it. The beef needs its own richness and moisture to stand beside a vegetable as powerful as a properly roasted Brussels sprout. Medium rare keeps both parties in conversation, each bringing its best qualities to the table.
ingredients: For the roasted crispy Brussels sprouts:
1 lb Brussels sprouts, trimmed and halved (or quartered if large)
For the shaved raw Brussels sprout salad:
½ lb Brussels sprouts, trimmed and very thinly shaved on a mandoline or with a knife
4 whole wheat buns, split and toasted
instructions: 1. Make the whole wheat buns: Dissolve yeast in warm water with honey. Let stand 5–10 minutes until foamy. In a stand mixer with dough hook, combine both flours and salt. Add yeast mixture, olive oil, and egg. Knead on medium 10 minutes until smooth and elastic. Place in an oiled bowl, cover, and rise 1½ hours until doubled.

2. Punch down dough and divide into 6 equal pieces. Shape into smooth balls, place on a parchment-lined baking sheet, cover, and proof 45 minutes. Preheat oven to 375°F. Brush with egg wash and sprinkle with rolled oats. Bake 18–20 minutes until golden and hollow-sounding when tapped on the bottom. Cool completely.

3. Make bacon-fat aioli: Cook bacon in a skillet over medium heat until crispy. Remove bacon to drain on paper towels (reserve for another use or crumble over burger). Carefully pour the rendered bacon fat into a small bowl and let cool to room temperature — do not refrigerate. Whisk together mayonnaise, 2 tbsp cooled bacon fat, apple cider vinegar, Dijon, and grated garlic. Season with salt and pepper. Refrigerate until needed.

4. Roast the Brussels sprouts: Preheat oven to 425°F. Toss halved Brussels sprouts with olive oil, salt, pepper, and garlic powder. Spread on a rimmed baking sheet in a single layer, cut-side down. Roast 20–25 minutes, flipping once halfway through, until deeply caramelized and crispy on the cut faces and outer leaves. In the last 2 minutes of roasting, drizzle with balsamic vinegar and honey and return to oven. Remove, toss with red pepper flakes, and taste for seasoning.

5. Make the shaved Brussels sprout salad: Combine olive oil, lemon juice, Dijon, honey, and grated garlic in a bowl. Whisk to emulsify and season with salt and pepper. Add shaved Brussels sprouts and toss to coat thoroughly. Let sit 10 minutes to slightly soften. Fold in shaved Pecorino.
6. Form patties: Gently mix ground beef with salt, pepper, and smoked paprika. Divide into 4 portions (about 6 oz each). Shape into ¾-inch-thick patties with a center dimple.

7. Cook patties: Heat a cast iron skillet or flat-top over high heat until smoking. Cook patties 3–4 minutes on the first side without pressing. Flip once. Add a slice of Swiss or Gruyère cheese to each patty. Cover and cook 1–2 more minutes until cheese is melted and internal temperature reaches 130–135°F for medium rare. Remove and rest 3 minutes.
8. Toast buns: Melt butter in a skillet over medium heat and toast buns cut-side down 2–3 minutes until golden.

9. Assemble: Spread bacon-fat aioli on both cut sides of each bun. Place the medium rare patty with melted cheese on the bottom bun. Add a small handful of the shaved Brussels sprout salad directly on top of the patty. Pile a generous heap of roasted crispy Brussels sprouts over the raw salad. Finish with flaky sea salt and a bit of fresh lemon zest. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately while the roasted sprouts are still crispy.
